Question: What are air fittings used for in trucks?
Answer: To connect components of the pneumatic system together. You’ll find them all over the vehicles wherever compressed air flows. For example, this one… Is two air fittings. There’s a crimp on fitting at each end of the hose, and a male-to-male fitting to connect the (female) hose end to the (female) inlet of the brake chamber. Unlike in my personal life, where I just go female to female and bypass any male connectors *drum roll*. You may find those types of fittings, you may find push-in fittings… … you may find compression fittings which crush a ferrel against the hose to keep the connection secure (not sure if this truck has any or not). Quiz time, kids… what’s specific about DOT brass and why is it so? If you mean an air coupler like those used for air tools… … (or conversely, you may see a valve core and stem like those used to inflate tires) that allows you to supply surrogate air (such as shop air, air from another truck, etc.) to the system and they’ll be used in conjunction with a ball valve or a one way check valve. For example, we do our own towing and recovery in-house. So if a tractor-trailer’s compressor craps out, and the complete unit has to be towed (or even just to separate the power unit from the trailer so another truck can take it), I can connect a hose from the emergency line glad hand if the wrecker to supply the pneumatic system of the casualty truck and just release the brakes with the MV3 valve rather than having to cage all the brake chambers and uncage them later on.

Question: 2001 Toyota Camry hesitates when accelerating and there is smoke coming from the fuel injector area. Could that be a failing fuel injector?
Answer: Smoke from a sealed fuel injector under a sealed valve cover? You saw all of that? That’s some serious x-ray vision! Not having such superpowers, I’d have to take the approach those of us in the mortal realm use, which is to put some actual effort into it. Now some people throw parts. Me, I prefer to diagnose. Just a quick foray to the Google machine tells me that your car has either a 2.2 liter 5S-FE inline four or a 1MZ-FE V6 engine. A little more perusing shows that these are electronically fired injectors. If they fail, you will most likely get a DTC indicating an issue with an injector, and a pretty good chance of misfire DTCs as well. Sense of smell helps here, as well. Smoke from fuel, oil, grease, rubber, and electrical all carries a distinct smell. What does the smoke smell like? Just at an educated guess, if you’re not getting a MIL and codes inviting injector issues, I’d be kinda inclined to suspect the problem to be electrical in nature, perhaps even an alternator. If the current is being disrupted, that could certainly cause hesitation in your Camry, which uses an electronic Throttle Position Sensor. But of course I could be right or wrong here… it’s all speculative on my end - educated speculation, but without doing a hands-on diagnosis, I can’t say, “yes, this is it/no, this definitely isn’t it”. I have serious doubts about it being your injectors though.

Question: Why is my car AC only working on 1, 2, 3 and not 4? 4 is the only one that works in my car and the AC light doesn’t turn on when I put it on 4. The car model is 2006 Nissan Xterra.

If you want more certainty, check for voltage in at the resistor inputs and if you don’t see voltage at the outputs, there’s your sign. Your highest blower setting doesn’t go through the resistor, which is why it’s unaffected. But it sounds like you may possibly be having issues beyond that or a different issue altogether.

Question: What features and specifications are most important to you when selecting a truck for your business, and how can a Mack Truck meet those needs to enhance your operations?

If you’re getting an AMT with the “Mack” engine, that’s what you end up with, else you get an Eaton with a Cummins… I don’t believe Mack offers the Allison TC10, but I could be mistaken. Manuals, the triple counter shaft Mack transmissions are much sturdier than the Eaton twin counter shaft manuals. The trade off being they’re a little more difficult (especially if you’re accustomed to the Eatons), and higher maintenance. If we were talking a truck that was operating in the woods, by all means the Mack transmissions. If we’re talking a highway truck, I’d opt for the Eaton or an AMT. Mack rears are what I’d want for an off highway application, but not for a highway application. Not to mention Mack won’t spec out a truck higher than ~430 hp with the 93 series and make you get either the 200 series or vendor axles. The 93s are heavy already, but the 200s, those are seriously heavy. Engines are Volvo engines with a different paint color and name on the valve cover. Support leaves a bit to be desired. If I were in the market, for me to specifically seek out a Mack truck, it would have to be because I wanted the Mack axles.
